source.title: Cross-Modal Redundancy and the Geometry of Vision-Language Embeddings
source.authors: Gr'egoire Dhimoila; Thomas Fel; Victor Boutin; A. Picard

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present; the text is not visibly garbled or cut off.
record.tranche_reason: Applies sparse autoencoders to vision-language foundation models and reports results about the features they recover, extending feature-dictionary analysis to this multimodal setting.
record.gate_note: The paper tests sparse feature dictionaries and their role in cross-modal structure in VLMs. It does not test the Toy Models of Superposition capacity claim, polysemanticity, feature completeness or canonicality, or whether represented features are intrinsically one-dimensional. Cited background claims are not treated as results. Rows below capture Table 1's modality-sensitive metrics; they do not establish recovery of ground-truth features in the foundation models.
record.test_reason: The paper mainly introduces an alignment-regularized SAE and uses it to study VLM embedding geometry. Its main Table 1 results are method comparisons on modality metrics, which bear on no version. It does test one version. In a synthetic ground-truth setting, a standard SAE fails to recover the true dictionary while an inductive-bias variant succeeds at the same reconstruction (R2 ≥ 0.99). The paper also argues that dictionaries with identical R2 can encode very different concept structures. Both bear on V5 (SAE features as canonical units).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that Iso-Energy-regularized SAEs reveal a compact bimodal subspace carrying cross-modal alignment, while unimodal atoms act as modality-specific biases explaining the modality gap. They say removing unimodal atoms closes the gap and bimodal-restricted arithmetic yields in-distribution edits. They also conclude that standard SAEs learn a diffuse mix despite similar reconstruction. The 'without harming performance' claim is softer in the appendix: on LAION, recall drops for smaller models (e.g. CLIP 0.882→0.760). Stated limitations are sensitivity to beta, analysis on SAE reconstructions, and dual-encoder models only.
record.recipe_differences: Uses Matching Pursuit sparse autoencoders, including an Iso-Energy alignment regularizer, to analyze VLM embeddings; it does not reproduce the Toy Models of Superposition method. The original sparse-superposition framework is discussed as background.
record.method_sensitivity: The alignment-penalty coefficient β matters: the paper reports little effect below β = 10−4 and degenerate solutions above β = 10−3 in its CLIP sweep. It says results are not very sensitive to the modality-score threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: With an Iso-Energy-regularized SAE, bimodal atoms carry nearly all cross-modal alignment (rho rises, e.g. 0.327→4.232 on CLIP). High-energy unimodal atoms act as modality biases explaining the modality gap.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In dual-encoder VLM embeddings, SAE atoms separate into unimodal bias atoms and a bimodal subspace that carries cross-modal alignment.

record.problems: The analysis is conducted on SAE reconstructions rather than original embeddings; the authors report sensitivity to β and limit experiments to dual-encoder VLMs. Table 1 provides no uncertainty estimates. The reported metrics are indirect evidence about feature organization and do not validate ground-truth or complete feature recovery in the foundation models.
record.rows_left_out: None from the selected Table 1 metrics.

untested.parts: No toy-model superposition experiment. There are no phase transitions, no geometry of features versus dimensions, and no sparsity sweep.
No test of capacity competition or of importance-driven dedicated dimensions.
No test of alternative causes of polysemanticity.

SAEs are used as a tool on VLM (not LLM) embeddings. Feature spreading across neurons is not measured, and the existence or recoverability of sparse features is not tested beyond qualitative feature galleries.
Completeness of SAE features and seed stability in the real VLMs are not directly tested.
No comparison of 1-D versus multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: Toy ground-truth dictionary recovery. When Iso-Energy is violated, SAE gets W=0.197 / mma=0.83 and SAE-A gets W=0.185 / mma=0.81. When it holds, SAE gets W=0.396 / mma=0.29 and SAE-A gets W=0.184 / mma=0.52.
missing.locator: Section 4 sanity check; Appendix C.2, Table 5a/5b

missing.what: Seed stability and coherence across SAE architectures on CLIP. Stability ranges 0.067–0.33; MP-SAE coherence is 0.99.
MP-SAE learns near-duplicate high-energy unimodal atoms (mean cosine >0.9, never co-activating), i.e. one direction split into many atoms.

record.verdict_notes: All Table 1 rows are the study's own method against an unregularized SAE on modality metrics, so none bears on a superposition version. The record's V4 supports and limits_scope labels are removed. The models are VLM dual encoders, not LLMs. The V5 verdicts rest on text and tables not captured as rows; see missing.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test feature dropping versus overlapping storage, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular geometry in toy networks.
Does not test whether polysemanticity arises from capacity competition or whether importance determines dedicated dimensions versus sharing.
Does not test alternative causes of polysemanticity or whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.
Tests SAE-derived sparse features in vision-language models, not LLMs generally; does not establish that the dictionaries recover all model features or that features are spread across neurons.
Does not establish SAE features as complete, stable, or canonical units of the original model representation.
Does not compare one-dimensional features with multidimensional features.

relationships.condition: Synthetic CLIP-like ground-truth data where Iso-Energy holds (tau1=0.999); MP-SAE with vs without alignment penalty
relationships.reason: From the text (no row). Standard SAE fails to recover ground-truth atoms (W=0.396, mma=0.29) while SAE-A succeeds (W=0.184, mma=0.52), both at R2≥0.99. Recovered units therefore depend on the SAE's inductive bias.
relationships.display_finding: The standard SAE failed to recover ground-truth atoms (W=0.396, mma=0.29) while SAE-A succeeded (W=0.184, mma=0.52), both at R2≥0.99, so the recovered units depended on the SAE's inductive bias.

relationships.condition: Real VLM embeddings (six dual encoders), SAE vs SAE-A at near-identical reconstruction
relationships.reason: From the text (no row). Authors say two dictionaries with identical R2 may encode very different concept structures. Standard SAEs learn a diffuse mix where SAE-A separates unimodal and bimodal atoms, so the decomposition is not canonical.
relationships.display_finding: At near-identical reconstruction, standard SAEs learned a diffuse mix while SAE-A separated unimodal and bimodal atoms; the authors note that dictionaries with identical R2 can encode very different concept structures.
